subsubtopic: INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION TO IMPLEMENT NEW TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Transport. Since it is now some three years since the federal and provincial ministers of transport in western Canada agreed upon the five major principles which affect transportation policy in western Canada, which was described as a breakthrough, since the government does not have now any legislation on the order paper to implement any of these principles-particularly as
Oral Questions
they relate to the redress of freight rate anomalies and to the incorporation of a new transportation policy in the form of legislation-can the minister tell the House if we can expect a modified version of Bill C-33 to be introduced in this session? Or are we simply to assume that the public will be treated to another list of pie in the sky promises similar to those which were floated during the election campaign of 1974?

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION TO IMPLEMENT NEW TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member for Vegreville said, we had Bill C-33 on the order paper in the last session. It was subjected to the beginnings of a filibuster, and as a result of consultation there was a clear indication that the filibuster would continue for a long time. That time was simply not available. If the hon. member would now give me an undertaking on the ease and speed with which the bill would be passed, I would be delighted to bring it forward now.
Bill C-33 contains extremely important measures in relation to the important issues of long-haul, short-haul and minimum-maximum freight rates so the railways cannot overcharge where people are captive in fact, although not in law. I think it is an important bill. I will be glad to have consultations with hon. members opposite, and if it looks as though we can move the bill forward, I will certainly bring it back immediately in the form it was in. If a modified form would speed things up, I would be delighted to do that, although 1 am afraid I would be running into two different views, even within the Conservative party, as to which modifications to make.

subsubtopic: INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION TO IMPLEMENT NEW TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, since the objections from this side of the House centred largely around the fact that the Minister of Transport wanted to set himself up as a transportation czar, and because the minister would not shake his nasty old habit of favouring the user-pay concept, this party took a very strong position against that bill. Unless the minister is prepared to modify those parts of the bill, we will again take a strong position against it. If the minister is not prepared to bring in legislation with those modifications, he should say so: he should come clean and tell the House what we can expect by way of a comprehensive set of legislative proposals to deal with the very serious problems which affect transportation in this country from coast to coast.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION TO IMPLEMENT NEW TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there was nothing in the bill which related to the so-called user-pay concept or any other such concept. Indeed, the only element which was of fundamental importance with regard to freight rates was an assurance that the user would not have to pay too much, which is, I would like the hon. member to know, a great concern of mine as well.
When the hon. member for Vegreville talked about interpreting certain clauses as setting up the Minister of Transport as a czar, he was giving an indication of the kind of filibuster that was being carried out, when in fact all the bill did in that regard was make it very clear that the minister would have to take responsibility for policy issues and not be deflected from

February 15, 1978
Oral Questions
his responsibility by the actions or role of the CTC. I think that is a very important principle.
However, the bill had complicated matters in it. It had in it some statements of principle, in clause 3, which were the result of discussions not only with western transport ministers but also with Atlantic transport ministers. Obviously, that clause was capable of a good deal of argument. I am quite prepared to come back without some of that material, if I can have some assurance that the clauses regarding long-haul, short-haul and maximum-minimum rates would be dealt with quickly in this House.

subsubtopic: INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION TO IMPLEMENT NEW TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext: Since it is important to provide a mechanism with which we can redress the anomaly of freight rates in this country, and since the third major priority of the new transportation policy as enunciated in the election campaign of 1974 is the removal of regional inequities in freight rates-and there has not been one freight rate change since that proclamation was made-are we to assume now, from what the minister is saying, that the government has abandoned the policy of removing inequities in regional freight rates? Is that what the minister is telling the House?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION TO IMPLEMENT NEW TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am telling the House and the hon. member exactly the opposite. The imposition of maximum rate control on the railways, so that they cannot charge whatever the market will bear in cases where they have a monopoly position, is very important to me. The hon. member is saying I should bring on the bill. If we bring in just those clauses which deal with that question, and if the hon. member says members of his party will not make 120 speeches about all the things which are left out and which were in Bill C-33,1 would be glad to do that. I will be glad to discuss this matter with the hon. member, and if we agree on being able very quickly to pass the clauses with regard to long-haul, short-haul and maximum-minimum rates, I will bring the bill before the House within two or three weeks.

subtopic: HALIFAX-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO REDUCE RATE FOR CONTAINERS
HALIFAX-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO REDUCE RATE FOR CONTAINERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to put at least one supplementary question to the Minister of Transport. I remind him that he has had four years to do something about inequities in the freight rate structure. A confidential report prepared by the Arthur D. Little firm in the United States, which was released within the last 24 hours in Halifax, indicates that the rate structure of CNR will very shortly price the port of Halifax out of the container business altogether unless something is done. That, in light of what the minister said, is a little hard to swallow.
We want to know when the minister is going to take his responsibility seriously and do something about the 115 per cent increase in the cost of moving containers out of the port of Halifax, and when he is going to do something positive to

enable the Atlantic provinces, the producers, processors and industrial interests, to compete in the central Canadian market, where they can no longer compete because of increasing freight rates.

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subtopic: HALIFAX-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO REDUCE RATE FOR CONTAINERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of Bill C-33 is to make sure that railways do not have complete freedom in rate setting in areas where they have practically monopoly control over freight movement. I say again to the hon. member, as I did to the hon. member for Vegreville, that if there is agreement to move forward with those provisions, I will be glad to bring them forward.
I should also point out that the thing we have to cure in the law is something which was overzealously done by a government some ten or twelve years ago, following upon a royal commission set up by a Conservative government. That was a mistake that I think we probably ought not to repeat on a subsequent occasion.

subtopic: HALIFAX-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO REDUCE RATE FOR CONTAINERS
speechtext: A final supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. That is the type of utter damn nonsense the people of Atlantic Canada will not put up with any longer from this government.

subtopic: HALIFAX-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO REDUCE RATE FOR CONTAINERS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: HALIFAX-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO REDUCE RATE FOR CONTAINERS
speechtext: Is the minister aware of the Arthur D. Little study? Is he aware of its implications? Does he agree with its conclusions? Also, can he tell the House why it was as cheap, three or four years ago, to move a container from Halifax to Chicago as it was to move it from Montreal to Chicago, and today the same container shipped from Halifax costs $500, as opposed to $350 from Montreal? Can the minister tell the Atlantic users of container service and our international customers who use the port of Halifax why that is the case, and why he is not directly responsible for it?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subtopic: HALIFAX-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO REDUCE RATE FOR CONTAINERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, perhaps it is not altogether obvious why at one time a rate should have been the same for a long distance as for a short distance. That is a principle that one would have to examine. In short, the reason freight rates are what they are is that after the MacPherson commission-set up by the right hon. member for Prince Albert-the minority parliament enacted legislation which gave, essentially, freedom to the railways to set rates on the principle of what the market would bear, on the theory that competition would control the situation.
I am convinced that competition, in many cases, cannot control the situation, because the mode of transportation may be completely limited to rail by the nature of the product and its movement. In such cases, we need additional protection- legislative protection. I have the instrument to do it, and I will be glad to see it supported when it comes forward.

Under the proposed amendment the judge can demand to see the document, in proceedings in camera, and examine it. If on the grounds of an affidavit filed by a minister he considers the matter as one against public policy, then he allows the document to be declared inadmissible. On the other hand, if he wants to clear up the secrecy of government, he admits the document.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF AGENCY TO SUPERVISE PIPELINE CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as reported at page 2815 of Hansard dated February 13, 1978, the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) said the following:
I want to say on behalf of this party that though we support the building of a pipeline it is apparent that the promises and conditions which were set forth on August 4 have not been implemented, and unless they are implemented we have very serious reservations about whether this legislation should be passed by the Parliament of Canada.
Yesterday the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Cros-bie) made a most convincing speech. Contrary to what the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) had to say, he emphasized the reservations pointed out by my colleague, the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands. In my preliminary remarks last night I quoted the questions asked by the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) and others in the official opposition about guarantees and sellouts. The hon. member for Yukon says that we cannot have guarantees. He agrees with the government position as stated by the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen) when he was answering a question in the House a few days ago. When the hon. member for Yukon says there is no sellout, I want to remind him that the hon. member for St. John's West interjected during the answer of the Deputy Prime Minister to the effect that in their negotiations with the United States they gave it all away. I concur with that statement. The government have been out-manoeuvred; they continue to tremble when they are negotiating with our friends south of the forty-ninth parallel.
With regard to the whole issue of our nationhood, our sovereignty and our being masters in our own house, I find it passing strange that our government can acquiesce to what is called generally competitive bidding for pipeline construction and any of the infrastructure which may be needed, such as pressure stations and so forth, while at the same time not only are our friends in the United States guaranteeing to protect their industry and their workers but countries in western Europe and Japan do the same thing.
February 15, 1978

The hon. member for Yukon says that if we were to do that it would be in violation of GATT. As my colleague, the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands, pointed out very accurately, there is nothing in GATT to prevent bilateral agreements or understandings. I want to illustrate this by citing the case of the Interprovincial Pipe and Steel Company in Regina and Edmonton, a Canadian company. Majority ownership in that company resides in the hands of the governments of Alberta and Saskatchewan and the company wants to do an $80 million expansion. DREE has been studying the case and has made reports. Now they are trying to make a decision on whether to approve that expansion. The problem is that the Interprovincial Pipe and Steel Company is caught in a Catch-22 situation. As I understand it, DREE is saying, on the one hand: "If you get contracts for the manufacture of the pipe, we will approve this expansion, and you will get $80 million in advance". On the other hand, the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce is saying: "If you can show us you have the capacity to make that pipe, you will get some contracts".
So there sits a Canadian company in western Canada which has a 2,000 or 3,000 mile advantage in North America in terms of manufacturing and delivering the pipe, which has the potential to provide a majority portion of the pipe for that 5,500 miles of pipeline, but which cannot exercise that advantage unless it can assure DREE that it will get the contracts, and it cannot assure DREE it will get the contracts until it can assure the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce and the Deputy Prime Minister that it has the capacity to produce the pipe.
If that is not a stacked deck against a Canadian company and against Canadian employment, I have never seen one. I would like to see who started all this about a high pressure, three quarter-inch pipe. Certainly it was not Ipsco, nor was it Stelco or Algoma. It was nobody here in the opposition and I do not know of anyone on the government side who could have started all this. But somehow or other the matter of having a high pressure, three quarter-inch pipe came up during the negotiations between Canada and the United States. There is no high pressure pipeline anywhere in North America, so far as I am aware, and there is no corporation capable of producing such a pipe, with the exception of one plant in Texas which can make a three quarter-inch pipe. It may well be that the U.S. steel industry has the capacity to move quickly into manufacturing that size of pipe, and if they have that capacity, one can hardly blame them for placing an unholy amount of pressure on the United States administration and on the U.S. Congress to arrange their dealings and negotiations with the government of Canada in such a manner that they will get a significant part of the action which they would get if there was a specification for a high pressure pipe.
Even if the National Energy Board were to come out with specifications which called for a low pressure pipe, under the terms of the agreement, in the phraseology of the minister's speech, in the government's statement and in the agreement about being generally competitive, the United States steel
Northern Pipeline
industry can be reasonably assured of a significant portion of the manufacture of the pipe. It would be interesting to know what chance, if any, Canadian steel pipe producers would have on contracts for this pipeline which is being made in Alaska or south of the 49th parallel. We can talk about general competitiveness all we like. The reality is the kinds of benefits which the public provides for the steel industry in the United States. Canadian contractors or Canadian bidders, the steel pipe manufacturers, if they were to bid competitively, do not have a chance of a snowball in hell of getting any of it.
I know of no other country which would allow itself to be made a new Panama. Once and for all Canada should stand up for Canadians, for Canadian workers and for Canadian industry. When will we have a federal government which will have the spine to do that? Even banana republics now stand up to the great U.S.A. They do not stand up with loaded guns or with the intention of starting wars. They are willing to be good neighbours. They are willing to help the U.S.A. out. But work done in Canada should be done by Canadians and controlled by Canadians. Canada should not, however, hold the project up for ransom with regard to prices.
Since 1867 we have had 46 years of Tories and 65 years of Liberals. They continue to betray our nationhood and undermine our capacity to do more and better. The Liberals and Tories bow at the altar of the Yankee dollar far more than any banana republic of third world country. They weep, moan and tremble, and if there is a difference with our friends south of the 49th parallel or if we want to do something the way we want to do it, somehow the old line parties feel that will destroy the great friendship and neighbourliness which exists between us and the United States. They feel that somehow any disagreement will harm investment. That is a myth which is continually perpetuated by members of the old line parties.
We must put guarantees into this legislation. We must insist that Foothills live up to what the government said on August 4, that there will be 90 per cent Canadian content. The Deputy Prime Minister is going to be in charge of this project. He says he is not interested in establishing a Canadian monopoly or cartel. It might be news to him, but neither are we. But we are determined that any project undertaken in Canada will be undertaken by Canadians. Any decision made should be the decision of this parliament, of our government, of the minister in charge of the project and of the company responsible for installing the pipeline. "Competition" means that United States industry will get a major portion of the benefit of this project. No self respecting Canadian member of parliament should hold still for that.
In addition, if any Canadian manufacturer or contractor is stupid enough to try to make unreasonable charges for the construction of this line, then and only then should contracts be open to competitive bidding. This could be provided for in the bill, or the minister could be authorized under the bill to make that decision. There are people in several government departments and certainly people with the Foothills company

February 15, 1978
Northern Pipeline
who know when there is unreasonable bidding. They can assess tenders from Ipsco or Stelco. They are not stupid.
The government is trying to tell us that there cannot be any guarantees because Canadian companies are dishonest and Canadian workers will be unreasonable. The government says that it must be possible for the Japanese to supply pipe and that it must be possible for steel plants in Pittsburgh, Chicago, Texas or elsewhere to supply pipe. The government has been out-manoeuvred. Unless these kinds of guarantees are put into the legislation, we will be another Panama.
I am trying to get in touch with Canadian companies who will tender on the installation of the pipeline to find out what they know about this, but I understand that there is in excess of $1.2 billion worth of pipeline construction equipment staged in the northwestern United States. It is left over from the construction of the Alaska pipeline. It has been written off. It has been bought and paid for. American contractors are buying it up or will buy it up at firesale prices, and they will submit competitive tenders for the construction of the pipeline in Canada. As far as I am aware, there is no Canadian company which will be able to compete against those kinds of tenders. We are not interested in getting fast bucks from American consumers of American gas. When Canada tries to help out a neighbour, we are interested in seeing that work done in Canada will be done by Canadians. There is no excuse for not saying that to our good friends south of the 49th parallel.
I am ashamed to say that our good friends to the south do not respect us. I do not want them to fear us. They have nothing to fear. But we do not get their respect because we do not have the courage to stand up for ourselves.
We have tried for many years to establish an industrial base to support the agricultural economy of western Canada. We have tried very hard, privately and publicly, but just when we get it going nicely opportunities to expand the industrial base further are poorly handled.
I want to invite the hon. member for Yukon to come with me on Friday to meet the board of directors of the Interprovincial Pipe and Steel Corporation. More particularly, I should like him to stand at the plant gate of Ipsco in Regina or in Edmonton and tell the steel workers that he agrees with the government that there should not be any guarantees in this legislation. I would like to see any Liberal or Tory candidate have the nerve to show up at either place during an election campaign. The meeting, I suggest, would not be political because not all the workers in those steel plants are NDP. But the workers will be angry. They will feel the same kind of shame that I feel as a Canadian when my government-even though I voted against them they are still my government- and my parliament allow what has been going on for decades to continue. The terrible price we are paying for being a branch plant country and the terrible price we are paying for unemployment was pointed out by my colleague, the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas),

on another issue several years ago when he said that because of our supine acquiescence we will always pay.
Mr. Speaker, there is nothing wrong with nationalism if it is positive nationalism, not the nineteenth century kind when countries used nationalism to exploit and defeat others. I mean a nationalism that has to do with our own nationhood, the kind that earns us the respect of our friendly neighbours. I mean the kind of nationalism that says to our friends in the United States, particularly when we have over a million people out of work: Look, we are happy to make Canadian soil available for a pipeline to take your gas from one part of your country to another, but on our soil the pipeline will be built by us, we will install it and put up the compressor stations. We will not overcharge and we will see to it that delivery of gas is secured. If we want to put some of our gas through parts of it ten of 20 years from now, there will be no problem.
We should not give away the store every time we deal with our friends the United States. A few years ago a senior officer of a United States operation told me: "The trouble with you Canadians is that you do not know what you want to do, how you want to do it, when and where you want to do it. I am getting sick and tired of you guys complaining about the Americans." In fact, the analogy he used was that of a hound dog sitting on a cactus, with all the spines sticking up his backside. Yet he is just too lazy to get off it, so he just sits there and howls.
If we do not grab this opportunity, Mr. Speaker, others will. Under this legislation others certainly will. Surely it is incumbent upon this parliament to put guarantees into the bill that the pipe will be manufactured in Canada, that the construction will be done by Canadian companies and that the installation of compressor stations and all the products needed for that will, as far as possible, be manufactured in Canada.
When the United States assisted the Soviet Union to instal the large pipeline that runs from the Soviet Union into eastern Europe, they provided technological help, construction foremen and private companies to help out. I never heard of the United States requesting competitive bidding on pipe. In fact, when Coca Cola puts up a plant in Africa or anywhere else it is African production, manufacture and labour that is used. Of course, Coca Cola gets a percentage of the profits but even those small countries stand up for themselves.
Sometimes there is disagreement, but even families disagree. Neighbours disagree. Sometimes neighbours do things you do not like. But you do not tell a neighbour that the next time he wants to put a lawn in you will do it for him and send him a bill. Countries are just the same, Mr. Speaker.
I do not think this legislation should pass in its present form. I do not think it should pass second reading unless and until the Deputy Prime Minister can assure this Elouse that guarantees will be placed in it at committee stage. Not only should there be guarantees of Canadian content, but in order to show our neighbourliness it should be provided in the legislation or in the regulations that excessive bidding or attempts by any Canadian company to extract more than is reasonable and just will be ruled out.
February 15, 1978

The hon. member for the Yukon and the Deputy Prime Minister have sounded like two of a kind in this debate, contrary to what the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) has said. When will they have the courage to say "Oh Canada, true north strong and free," and to say it in a manner that demonstrates belief in the words? I have a great deal of regard for the Deputy Prime Minister. Nationhood may mean something different to each of us but it is extremely important. It is not a question of whether a steel plant in Regina makes 2,000 miles of pipe. It goes beyond that-

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF AGENCY TO SUPERVISE PIPELINE CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at First glance this bill strikes me as fulfilling the yearnings of most Canadians in two vital sectors of our community, that is energy and labour. We know that the purpose of the bill is to make available to Canadians in the shortest possible time and at the best prices the energy resources which are found in the Mackenzie delta. We also know that the bill promotes the construction of a pipeline by free enterprise, an undertaking which will no doubt create tens of thousands of jobs in Canada, whatever reservations members opposite may entertain about it.
This negative position taken by the parties opposite is not new. However, under the present circumstances, Mr. Speaker, I am quite surprised. As soon as we learn that Statistics Canada has published the monthly unemployment rate as soon as we hear about a lay-off in a Canadian plant, we see members opposite, especially from the NDP, blaming and criticizing the government for doing nothing to create employment. Yet we have here a bill which is historic, a great bill through which we intend to create many thousands of jobs in Canada. Perhaps the fact that we saw Fit to leave to private enterprise the responsibility of making this important project a reality was contrary to the philosophy of the NDP, but given our current economic predicament I would have thought those people intelligent enough to accept and recognize that the government is making a concerted effort towards job creation to help Canadians and improve our economy. Moreover, Mr. Speaker, this pessimistic attitude on the part of the New Democratic Party in particular is indeed an insult to our industry and to Canadian workers. I do not understand the lack of confidence of the members of that party in the ability
Northern Pipeline
of our industry and workers to compete with other countries in the making of pipes for the pipeline. I see there a token of small-mindedness and an overt lack of self-confidence.
For instance, would they want to include a clause stipulating that only Canadian industry can bid on the Canadian section of the pipeline, thereby excluding industry and our workers from participation in the construction of the American section of the pipeline? In order to provide for such a possibility, it is necessary to have an open mind and to be confident in one's own capabilities. I wish the members of the New Democratic Party would think about that and realize that we have anticipated that possibility to allow our industry, which is perfectly able to compete with the American industry, to participate not only in the construction of the Canadian section of the pipeline which is proposed in this bill, but also in the construction of the American section as well.
But it is mostly the negative attitude on the part of the NDP that I noticed, in spite of the loud protests from the hon. member who just spoke and who does not seem to understand what I am telling him. I accuse them of being unrealistic and inconsistent. I believe they seem to ignore that what they are advocating would likely preclude this agreement between Canada and the United States on the construction of the pipeline. So, were it not for this agreement and the legislation before us, there would not be any job creation in that sector in Canada. What they preach today by way of their futile protests is unrealistic. If we were to believe them and implement what they preach today, the United States would never have accepted the construction of the pipeline without any consideration for the cost. And ir. that sense, I say that the NDP in particular is being unrealistic and irresponsible.
Last night, I listened to the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) who, in his monologue-to use a polite expression-was saying: But I for one intend to see to it that this debate keeps on going for three or four weeks on second reading if need be, because an amount of $10 billion is at stake, and I intend to take part in the discussion in committee to talk at the report stage and also to participate in the debate on third reading so that we take as much time as possible to study this bill because $10 billion is involved I am afraid he did not read the bill: the pipeline is not paid by the Canadian government, by Canadian taxes but the entire building cost is paid by private enterprise. After the few days of debate we had on second reading of this important piece of legislation, I feel that members of the official opposition did not read the bill and do not know its contents as regards a certain guarantee for Canadian participation and the beneficial effect it will have on energy consumption in Canada and job creation.
Therefore, I think it is advisable in this context to refer this bill to committee and to highlight the main points in the hope that this will have the effect of avoiding statements which are not based on reality and which do not take the needs of the Canadian people into consideration during these times when we have an urgent need of new jobs and must act quickly to get the most out of our energy resources.

February 15, 1978
Northern Pipeline
Mr. Speaker, this is an historic bill which we are now discussing on second reading. Its purpose is to authorize Canada legally to co-operate with the United States in the achievement of what the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mac-Eachen) rightly called yesterday in the House one of the most ambitious projects ever undertaken by private enterprise. Bill C-25 provides for the construction in the north of a $10 billion pipeline, of some 5,500 miles which will be used to transport natural gas from the Arctic to meet the pressing needs of millions of consumers in the two countries, Canada and the United States. This bill therefore authorizes the construction of a northern gas pipeline, as stipulated in the Canadian and American agreement; in addition, it provides for the setting up of the Northern Pipeline Agency to formulate and supervise the plans with a view, first of all, to maximizing the economic benefits of the project for Canada and, second, to minimizing its adverse effects of social and ecological nature.
The Deputy Prime Minister and President of Privy Council is the minister responsible for this bill in his capacity as chairman of the special cabinet committee on the pipeline. How right he was in saying that this huge joint project, which passing of this bill will allow, will stimulate considerably both production and employment in Canada, will help to achieve the objective of becoming self-sufficient in the field of energy, by giving access at a reasonable cost to the main new reserves of natural gas in the Mackenzie Delta.
I would recall, Mr. Speaker, that near the end of last year the American Congress approved by a strong majority similar proposals brought forward by President Carter for the implementation of the bilateral agreement signed by our two countries.
I think it can be useful at this stage to give a brief description of the pipeline to show its importance as well as a number of statistics and to indicate its cost. The pipeline will start at Prudhoe Bay, Alaska, and will go south to Yukon. This of course is the American section which will run for 731 miles. Then the pipeline will go from the Alaska boundary to Whitehorse, Yukon, which is the site of the proposed 737-mile lateral spur which will reach the Mackenzie delta where our natural gas resources are. Later it will cross the northeast part of British Columbia, heading southeast, through Alberta, up to James River, near Caroline. The pipeline will then divide into two sections: the western leg, up to Kingsgate, British Columbia, and the eastern leg up to Monchy, Saskatchewan. The pipeline, including the Delta lateral, will stretch over a total distance of 2,765 miles in Canada. In the 48 continental states of the U.S., the Pacific Gas Transmission Company and the Pacific Gas and Electric Company will undertake to build the western section going down to California, which will parallel the present system, and the Northern Border Company will build the eastern section to the central western states, for a total length of 1,991 miles.
So the pipeline, including the Dempster lateral going to the Mackenzie delta, will cover a total distance of 5,487 miles

over Canadian and American land. It will cost approximately $10 billion. The Alaska section is estimated at $3.5 billion, the Canadian section, except for the Dempster lateral, will cost about $4.2 billion and, in the 48 continental states, $2.3 billion.
Mr. Speaker, it is expected that in the beginning the complete system will carry up to 2.4 billion cubic feet per day of American gas, and up to 1.2 billion cubic feet of Canadian gas.
According to the work schedule, Mr. Speaker, construction of the pipeline, in northern British Columbia, that is on the Canadian side, would not start before the winter of 1980-81, and under the Canada-U.S. agreement, construction would not start in the Yukon before January 1, 1981, as the deadline for the system being operational is January 1, 1983.
The proposed Northern Pipeline Agency will work in close co-operation with the National Energy Board, and will serve as the only regulatory agency in charge of all federal responsibilities with regard to the Canadian part of the pipeline. Under this legislation, a member of the National Energy Board would be sent to the agency as designated officer, and the board will delegate to him the authority to exercise certain of its powers as regards the project, subject to the approval of the responsible minister and the general power of direction of the governor in council.
The deputy head of the agency will be the commissioner whose head office will be in Ottawa. He will be the minister's principal advisor on matters of policy. An administrator whose head office will be in Calgary will be responsible for the routine administrative duties, within the authority delegated to him by the minister. He will report to the minister through the commissioner, and the designated officer of the National Energy Board may be appointed administrator or deputy to the administrator.
Mr. Speaker, for the purposes of the pipeline, the bill authorizes the governor in council to transfer to this agency the legislative powers now exercised by several other departments and agencies, which must ensure that the relevant federal responsibilities fall under a single regulatory agency. The bill also proposes amendments to a number of acts to facilitate the accomplishment of this objective, as well as the rapid construction of the pipeline in this country.
Moreover, the legislation replaces all certificates of public convenience and necessity certificates required to authorize the project. It should be noted, Mr. Speaker, that the Foothills group will have to comply with the many conditions set out in the legislation. The plans and specifications, the exact route taken by the network, as well as other matters, such as the location and the nature of temporary camps and the training and employment requirements of northern residents will all be submitted to the approval of federal authorities.
The group will have to prove to the satisfaction of the minister responsible for the administration of the pipeline and the National Energy Board that it has obtained the financing required for building the network and has adequately ensured against the risk of incompletion. Foothills will have to meet all
February 15, 1978

the commitments made during the hearings of the National Energy Board which aimed at maximizing the economic benefits of the project and minimizing its social, economic and environmental negative impacts. In addition, it will have to comply with other specific conditions to be established under the legislation by the designated administration officer. These policies, instructions and orders will be subject in certain cases to additional studies that the company will have to make, such as that on the statement of environmental effects that it has already begun as part of the second stage of the examination process in this area. The detailed conditions will first of all be published in draft form to enable the public to examine and comment on them before they are given final approval by the designated administration officer.
The terms and conditions of implementation also give specific details about the comprehensive information that Foothills will be asked to submit to the approval of the administration concerning its hiring and supply plans. These provisions aim at ensuring that the Canadian staff and suppliers will have an opportunity to offer the goods and services required for carrying out the project in compliance with the objective of Foothills to ensure approximately 90 per cent Canadian content. Moreover, under the conditions set out in the legislation, Foothills will have to increase the capacity of the main pipe if necessary for carrying Canadian gas from the Mackenzie delta once the Dempster link is completed, in order that these new reserves may supply Canada's increasing energy needs in future years.
Mr. Speaker, this legislation empowers the minister to hold consultations with the United States government and Canadian provinces and territories when needed, to coordinate all aspects of the project involving various jurisdictions.
The legislation also provides for a Federal-Provincial Consultative Council to meet as required and which will be charged with strengthening day to day liaison and co-ordination between officials of various governments charged with overseeing the pipeline project.
The bill also authorizes the establishment of one or more advisory councils consisting of not more than ten members from outside the government to ensure communications and consultations between the various public groups involved and the Northern Pipeline Agency.
As the Deputy Prime Minister pointed out the Yukon has already shown it was interested in the establishment of such a council, which will give the general public a well-organized forum to make its views known on the nature of implementation parameters that are in the Yukon's best interest. The legislation amends the National Energy Board Act to permit the board to recover from any corporation the costs incurred by the regulations agency in overseeing and surveying the planning and construction of any pipeline from the issue of a certificate until one year after leave to operate the facility has been granted. Under that amendment, Foothills will bear the costs incurred by the Northern Pipeline Agency and the board in overseeing and surveying the project, from the day the act is made applicable until one year after the project has been
Northern Pipeline
opened. And that aspect seems very important to me. Not so long ago in this Flouse, on an opposition day, some members, especially from the Conservative side, called for the creation of Crown agencies or corporations of a temporary nature and at the lowest cost possible.
Now, we have here an example of an agency which is set up for a limited time, as I have just explained, and furthermore its cost is fully borne by private enterprise without any charge to the treasury. So 1 think that in addition to attaining all the major aims I mentioned previously, the fact that this type of temporary agency grouping in a rational manner of some elements of various other departments involved in this tremendous project, and above all, that its cost will be borne by private enterprise is in my opinion an innovation and at least meets the wishes of many government and opposition members. When it considers the matter of tolls and tariffs, the National Energy Board should take into account the relevant clauses of the Canada-U.S. agreement. The bill also authorizes the governor in council to make regulations regarding the tolls and tariffs in order to implement this agreement and prescribe the method by which the Board will establish a rate of return on equity investment in the project. Another clause suggests that the National Energy Board Act be amended so that the definition of tolls may be changed. As a result, the NEB will be authorized to collect such charges when the pipeline is ready to transmit oil or gas. This bill provides for the repeal, one year after the issue of the licence to operate the pipeline, of those sections of the act establishing the Northern Pipeline Agency and delegating to it as well as to designated officials certain powers. I stressed this point earlier.
Flowever, those sections may be repealed by a joint resolution of both Houses of Parliament if a certificate of public convenience and necessity is issued for the construction of the Dempster spur before the authority to operate the main system is granted. Mr. Speaker, the Deputy Prime Minister explained that this line of action had been taken because it was considered prudent to provide for the dissolution of the agency one year after the beginning of the operation of the main system in case no certificate would have been issued for the Dempster spur which would be the only reason justifying the retention of the regulating body. That method also leaves parliament the choice to authorize the agency to undertake the responsibility for the planning and the monitoring of the Dempster spur if the required certificate is issued within the prescribed time period.
This bill will impose an impressive set of terms and conditions for the proposed northern pipeline to be built by the Foothills group to carry Canadian and U.S. natural gas from the Arctic to southern markets. This bill on the northern pipeline specifically requires participating companies to meet general conditions relating to varied matters such as the procurement of Canadian labour, goods and services, the design, specifications and route of the system, the elimination or reduction of adverse socioeconomic and environmental effects.
2894

February 15, 1978
Northern Pipeline
Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, the companies will have to provide detailed information on things such as costs, financing plans, contracts to manufacturers and shippers, operation and security guidelines, collective agreements, and, in many cases, they will be required to secure the approval of the federal government. The general terms set out in the bill will be complemented afterward by orders, guidelines and specific requirements, the proposed drafts of which setting out the conditions in detail should be made public early this summer so the public will be able to comment on them before they are put into effect.
The policies dealing with the procurement of goods and services needed for the construction try to maintain a good balance between two crucial objectives: first, the maximm input from Canadian industry, second, the construction of the pipeline in Canada at the lowest possible cost.
The reasons we want to maximize Canadian input are obvious, but we must take into account the fact that Canadian gas consumers want the construction of the pipeline to be as efficient and economical as possible.
The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen) made that statement when he tabled this bill for second reading.
According to the bilateral agreement signed with the United States, Canada is directly interested to limit costs. U.S. users will have to pay the total transportation costs for Canadian gas on the Dempster lateral that willl be 277 miles long if the total expenses for the main pipeline built in Canada do not exceed estimated cost by more than 35 per cent. If they do the U.S. share will be reduced accordingly.
It was interesting to hear the minister state and I quote:
Except for that particular point, Canadian consumers are to be more directly affected by the total cost of the system and the delivery cost, for it is expected that by the mid-1980s, Canadian Arctic gas will meet some 10 per cent of our requirements while Alaskan gas is expected to meet only 5 per cent of U.S. demand.
It should be noted that the Foothills group is required, under the terms and conditions specified in the bill, to submit a procurement program covering all goods and services for the approval of the minister responsible. This program must be aimed at achieving the maximum level of Canadian input for the supply of goods and services and maximum advantage should be taken of opportunities to foster Canadian research and promote the long-term expansion of viable Canadian suppliers.
The company is required to submit to the minister the outline of the procedure it intends to follow to carry out its Canadian goods and services procurement program. Once the minister has approved the goods and services procurement plan, the company will be required to carry it out under the pipeline agency supervision. Some proposed contracts, specified by the minister, would have to be approved by the minister before being awarded. If the minister has reasons to believe that a proposed contract with a foreign supplier could result in sales losses or unfair trade practices, he may request the company to produce proof to the contrary before giving his authorization.
Foothills will also be required to obtain the minister's approval of a detailed manpower plan designed to ensure maximum possible use of Canadian labour in the planning construction and operation of the pipeline. According to the general conditions outlined in the bill, Foothills must also comply with the undertakings given to the National Energy Board regarding social and economic matters, problems concerning ecology, animal life, fisheries and farm lands and act toward solving them as well as comply with any other direction made by the designated officer of the pipeline agency.
All these requirements will be recapitulated in the detailed conditions issued pursuant to the general provisions of the bill after having been reviewed thoroughly and submitted to the public for its comments. Moreover, Foothills must seek the minister and the National Energy Board approval for the network plan, including pipe diameter, wall thickness, and maximum allowable pressures. It must also have the final plan for each section approved by the designated officer of the pipeline agency, submit detailed estimates on the cost of these sections and prepare an operation and security guide and inspection plans to the satisfaction of the National Energy Board.
The companies participating in the work are also bound, under the general terms and conditions, to file with the minister and the National Energy Board, documents establishing satisfactorily that a source of financing has been found, that debt instruments do not contain any provision requiring the consent of their holders to the financing of the Dempster line, and that the major part of the financing is Canadian, within the terms of the Foreign Investment Review Act. Foothills must also convince the minister and the National Energy Board that it is protected against any risk of non-com-pleton of the pipeline and interruption of its construction. To comply with its commitments and the Canadian and American agreement, Foothills is also bound, pursuant to the provisions of the bill, to construct the spurs required to transmit the gas to remote communities along the main pipeline. It will have to spend up to $5 million to build the secondary lines needed to distribute gas in the Yukon.
To conclude, Mr. Speaker, I am convinced that this vast endeavour will generate considerable benefits, over both the short and the long terms, for all Canadians. First, it will give us access to a new and important source of energy, at once more sure and more economical than any other; second, it will stimulate considerably both production and employment in many parts of the country; third, it will certainly have a bearing on our international balance of payments; and four, it will play a vital role in the long term development of our northern economy. That having been said, and those specific details given, I therefore hope, in the interest of all Canadians, that the parties of the opposition will facilitate the adoption of this important bill as soon as possible.

February 15, 1978

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF AGENCY TO SUPERVISE PIPELINE CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to say at the outset that I am delighted to make a brief intervention in this most important debate. It is not my intention to review the importance of the pipeline, which has been adequately described by my colleagues, the deficiencies, which have as well been described by hon. members, or, indeed, many of the positive proposals suggested by those on this side who spoke earlier in the debate. I want to concentrate on the specific issue of land claims in the Yukon which the minister indicated yesterday was a specifically important factor relating to the pipeline, and in particular to the people who live in the north and who are really the most directly affected by the project.
I listened with great interest and, I must say, astonishment yesterday to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Faulkner). Let me make two or three observations-and there are many I could make-in relation to the speech he made in this House.
First, in spite of the minister's attempt to emasculate the government's position on a second stage inquiry, which was promised by a previous minister of Indian affairs and northern development and, indeed, Dean Lysyk when he was in the communities of the Yukon, who pointed out very clearly that there would be a second stage inquiry, there is no doubt in my mind that the minister has not changed his position and that in fact there is still no promise of a second stage inquiry.
Second, if I understood the minister correctly I am sure he was suggesting that land claims represented a most important component in this entire debate. He also gave the impression to this House of Commons that negotiations were proceeding very smoothly, that there were no problems with negotiations, and implied they were almost on the verge of obtaining a settlement with the native people of the Yukon territory. That just does not live up to the facts.
As you may recall, Mr. Speaker, the Council of Yukon Indians was in Ottawa not too long ago discussing the problems it was having with this government relating to the pipeline issue, specifically the problems in respect of land claims. Let me quote from page 3 of this press release:
We are now faced with some clear choices. We can continue to oppose a pipeline until our land claims are settled and be labelled as radical and anti-development. Or, we can compromise, thereby, sacrificing our rights to self-determination on our home land.
We have decided not to compromise but to fight!
We will take our case to the Canadian people. We will demonstrate the humanity and justness of our position. We will use every legal means at our disposal to ensure that we achieve a fair and just settlement. On February 13, the Federal Court will rule on our opposition to the National Energy Board recommendations. Our struggle to achieve self-determination will not stop there.
All I can say is that that does not sound to me as though negotiations are proceeding smoothly, and it does not sound to me as though they are on the verge of agreement in principle.

speechtext:
I realize that, but that statement to me is self-explanatory of the situation that exists in the Yukon.
Another very brief comment that astonished me yesterday was the statement by the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development as recorded at page 2846 of Hansard, in which he indicated very clearly the position in respect of the $50 million which had been suggested in the Lysyk report and by other members on this side. The minister stated:
I informed the Council for Yukon Indians last November that we are prepared to give very serious consideration to a proposal whereby such a fund would be established as soon as an agreement in principle was reached.
This is astonishing because somewhat earlier, in the Globe and Mail of January 25, there appeared an article entitled "Ottawa acts to speed land claims", in which reference was made to a $50-million advance into a Yukon native trust; but there was nothing about an agreement in principle. This is a brand new concept the minister introduced into the debate yesterday. This is one of the difficulties we have experienced, and certainly that the native people have experienced in the Yukon vis-a-vis their relationship with this government.
When Canada and the United States signed an agreement in principle applicable to the northern natural gas pipeline they signed a death warrant to the way of life in the Yukon. Whether Yukoners view the pipeline as synonymous with progress with no significant adverse effects, whether they view the pipeline as an evil intrusion of southern influence which will disrupt and permanently change one of the few remaining frontiers, or whether they accept the inevitability of development providing certain conditions are adhered to, they all agree that significant changes are inevitable with the construction of a pipeline. With the introduction of the legislation the federal government, whether by accident or design, has polarized and hardened the position of Yukoners.
The pipeline may be an engineering feat unexcelled in the world. It may be a success in delivering gas to the United States, and there are undoubtedly economic benefits that will accrue to Canada, with convincing arguments that job opportunities are significantly important at a time when the number of unemployed in Canada rivals that of the depression years. But however valid these or other reasons for the construction of a pipeline may be, these potential gains may be overshadowed by discontent and divisiveness in the Yukon unless the government acts responsibly to create harmonious relations between all the segments of society in the Yukon. I am not convinced that the government of Canada recognizes the significance or magnitude of this particular problem. More importantly, sir, there is little tangible evidence that the government cares about the individual whose home is in the Yukon.
This government's record to date in dealing with the native people has been virtually non-productive in spite of the fact that negotiations of land claims have been underway since 1973. In addition, the constant feuding with the territorial council and other responsible groups in the Yukon has bred discontent. The government's insensitive attitude to the wishes of all Yukoners, native and white alike, will be aggravated as
80031 -42Vi

February 15, 1978
Northern Pipeline
the various agencies become more preoccupied with the design and construction of the pipeline. This will occur at the expense of the issues that are potentially divisive among the people of the Yukon.
The implications of the problem were prophetically described in the document "Together Today for Our Children Tomorrow" by the Yukon Indian people, who state at the beginning of the chapter entitled "Today":
In 1973 the picture of the Yukon Indians is not a pretty one. The Yukon Indian people are not a happy people. Both the white man and the Indian are becoming more and more disgusted with each other. The communications gap, the social gap, the economic gap-all these are widening. Both Indian and white are getting nervous because of the lack of understanding and tolerance among both groups.
To a great extent, a good deal of the uncertainty that exists in the Yukon is related to the government's handling of the comprehensive land claims and the ability to arrive at a just and equitable settlement. Let me emphasize, if I may, the importance of this issue of land claims and their settlement. Mr. Justice Berger during his inquiry in the Northwest Territories in relation to the Mackenzie Valley pipeline made a comment that is relative to the situation in the Yukon when he stated:
If the pipeline is approved before a settlement of claims takes place, the future of the north-and the place of the native people in the north-will in effect, have been decided for them.
In his report entitled "Alaska Highway Pipeline Inquiry", Dean Lysyk indicated that native land claims was a major issue. In part, it reads:
With respect to the Yukon Indian land claim, we should like to emphasize that, contrary to the expectation of some observers, there is no significant element of public opinion in the Yukon that either challenges the validity of this land claim or doubts that it is important and desirable to settle the claim quickly and justly. Everyone understands that the settlement of the Indian land claim will not merely prepare the way for future economic developments that may be financed from southern Canada, but that substantial financial resources and the specified rights that will be placed in the hands of the Indian people will, of themselves, provide a strong and long-lasting stimulus to the local economy that cannot fail to be of benefit to everyone living in the Yukon.
In preparing its position paper entitled "Meaningful Government for all Yukoners", the government of the Yukon Territory clearly recognized the validity of native land claims. The introduction to that document reads as follows:
The object of this paper is to discuss how government in the Yukon Territory can be made more meaningful to all residents, native and non-native alike. This entire package is a necessary element that must be considered along with other aspects of the Indian land claims negotiations.
It continued:
In this paper there is no discussion on the Indian corporations which will be concerned with controlling and developing any assets that native people will receive. Nor is there discussion on other native organizations that may be concerned with aspects of Indian culture, society and human resource development. This is because these areas are primarily of native interest and the governments should not be directly involved with them although assistance should be available if necessary.
Mr. Robert Blair, the president and chief executive officer of the Alberta Gas Trunk Line Company and Foothills Pipe Lines Ltd.-the company responsible for building the Canadi-

an portion of the Alcan pipeline-spoke of the rights of northern native residents during the hearings before the National Energy Board. On November 8, 1976, he stated:
I feel sure that the issue of "land claims" alone will be a factor of great importance to the timing of a Mackenzie Valley pipeline and is a factor whose effect on timing has not been quantified at all successfully. I put the words "land claims" in quotation marks because this factor is far more; it is the determination of the residential and employment and economic rights of the majority of the permanent residents of the large part of Canada through which a Mackenzie Valley route would proceed. I have personally given considerable time to work on this factor.
While appearing before the National Energy Board on December 10, 1976, he stated:
You don't ride over the citizens to push through an industrial development.
Also on the same date he stated:
Until there is settlement of those matters, 1 do not believe that a manageable project can be carried out.
In its report, the National Energy Board emphasized that the settlement of comprehensive land claims was a major factor in the construction of a pipeline.
The observations in support of the settlement of land claims by the previous individuals and groups I have mentioned is by no means complete. I am sure many more could be added. I assume it provides sufficient background evidence to support the very obvious fact that the federal government should honour its commitment to settle the native land claims in the Yukon. The government should have been acting in a far more responsible manner to achieve that end.
Why the delay? Why so little progress in view of the fact that negotiations commenced in 1973? Obviously it is to the advantage of the native people to arrive at a just and equitable settlement before the onslaught of a major development project in the north. The reasons revolve around two basic issues, namely, mistrust and the deliberate attempt of the federal government to slow the progress of the negotiations to serve its own political ends.
In 1969, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) introduced the controversial white paper on Indian policy which rejected aboriginal rights. Despite the fact the white paper was withdrawn following intense reaction from the Indian community across Canada, and the Prime Minister was forced to qualify his position on aboriginal rights following the supreme court decision on the Nishga case in 1973, the Indians across Canada continue to distrust the motives of the present Liberal government. The concern of the native people was reinforced when the federal government assumed a very passive role, abrogating its constitutional responsibilities in the James Bay agreement.
In 1972 the Grand Council of the Cree were attempting to negotiate with the Quebec government following the proposed James Bay hydroelectric project. The Quebec Boundaries Extension Act of 1912 clearly indicated negotiations should take place, and yet the federal government refused to intervene despite its constitutional authority under the British North America Act. When the negotiations failed, the Grand Council of the Cree and the Northern Quebec Inuit Association took
February 15, 1978

the James Bay corporation to court. Following lengthy trial proceedings, once again they returned to the negotiating table. In a restricted time frame, the Cree and the Northern Quebec Inuit Association were confronted by the James Bay Power Corporation, the James Bay Development Company, Hydro Quebec, and the province of Quebec. Although the federal government was a party to the negotiations, it failed to intervene and counteract the adversary role of the large corporations.
On one occasion just prior to the deadline for the signing, I was asked by the Northern Quebec Inuit Association to seek a one month extension of the negotiations. That extension was not to negotiate a Five-cent per hour raise; it was to negotiate the lifestyles and entire future of Eskimos in northern Quebec. The following day I asked a question in the House and I was refused by the then minister of Indian affairs and northern development. He refused to grant a one month extension.
When Eskimos in the northern part of Quebec were experiencing grave difficulty in Finalizing their land selection, once again the federal government refused to take action to protect the interests of the Inuit. The most devastating testimony regarding the lack of concern on the part of the federal government with respect to native rights was its refusal to insert a clause in the bill which would protect the rights of non-signatories to the agreement.
Subsequent testimony during the hearings of the standing committee clearly identified a number of Indian, native and Inuit people who perhaps had rights to that area. The argument was very simple: if the group had aboriginal rights, then a grave injustice was being carried out by extinguishing those rights unilaterally. Yet a simple amendment which would have extinguished the rights of those signing the agreement and protected the rights of others who may or may not have a claim to the area was defeated by the government. Is it any wonder that the native community across Canada mistrusts the government?
It was in the context of this background that the document entitled "Together Today For Our Children Tomorrow" was presented to the government in 1973. The Prime Minister's initial response was positive, yet negotiations between the Council of Yukon Indians and the federal government was painfully slow. Federal negotiators refused to respond to that detailed document. In reality, those negotiators had no authority to negotiate unless they had clearance from Ottawa.
On March 3, 1975 the former Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, the present Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Goyer), arrived in Whitehorse and made a unilateral public offer of settlement. The government knew this announcement violated the negotiating process, and not unexpectedly the native people rejected the offer and the methods employed by the government.
Nego'iations remained in limbo despite pressure from the Council of Yukon Indians. Finally in October of 1975, the minister appointed a one-man negotiating team, Mr. Digby
Northern Pipeline
Hunt, the former assistant deputy minister of northern development.

He was one of a small group of federal architects which had been formed to develop, prepare for, and promote the Mackenzie Valley pipeline.
Although the second round of negotiations commenced, they were clouded with uncertainty. Because of his background and involvement in northern pipeline development, Mr. Hunt's appointment was viewed with suspicion. Concern about his appointment to this important position fell on deaf ears in the government and our fears that additional time would be wasted in settling the land claims became a reality with the suspension of negotiations in 1976.
Negotiations commenced for a third time in 1977 and on July 19, 1977, the former Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, the present Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Allmand), reported from Ottawa substantial progress with Yukon Indian claims. The report, which I think is very significant, stated the following:
Indian and Northern Affairs Minister Warren Allmand stated today that he was very encouraged by the release Friday, July 15, of a "settlement model" for the Yukon Indian claim. The model was made public by the Planning Council for the Yukon Indian claim, following lengthy discussion between planning council members who consist of representatives of the Council for Yukon Indians, the government of Canada and the Yukon territorial government. The model describes the goals of the Yukon Indians and outlines ways in which they could be achieved. "This is a significant step forward in the resolution of the Yukon Indian claim".
The former Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development said:
I am confident that the settlement model, which has my personal endorsement as well as that of the board of directors of the Council for Yukon Indians and the executive committee of the Yukon territorial government, will lead to an agreement in principle and ultimately to a final agreement.
The minister said he had been following the Yukon discussions closely through his special representative and the federal negotiator, Dr. J. K. Naysmith, and he emphasized the value of the "co-operative planning process" which has provided an effective framework for reaching agreement. He said:
The preparation of this settlement model is proof of the substantial progress that has been made by the Council for Yukon Indians and the two levels of government by co-operating and dealing openly with the issues involved.
He said also:
The process could well serve as an example of how complex elements in native claims might be handled in other parts of Canada.
The minister was optimistic that an agreement in principle between the Yukon Indians and government may be reached by the end of 1977. He reiterated his position that the resolution of the Yukon Indian claim is a high priority with the government and that every effort must be made to resolve it in an equitable and realistic manner.
Where is the agreement in principle that was promised by the end of 1977? Why have negotiations stalled once again? Are we to believe the resolution of the Yukon Indian claim is a high priority with this government?

February 15, 1978
Northern Pipeline
In light of events in recent months, broken promises, loss of trust and inevitable confrontation, the obvious conclusion is that the Yukon land claim is not a priority but an issue to be engulfed by the gigantic pipeline project as it gains momentum. We witnessed a similar struggle with the James Bay agreement, and this government, by virtue of its actions in the recent past, has set the stage to impose its will rather than honouring its commitment and constitutional responsibility to negotiate a fair and equitable agreement.
On April 19, 1977, the former minister of Indian affairs and northern development announced the establishment of a board of inquiry on the socioeconomic aspects of the proposed Alaska Highway gas pipeline. The board was chaired by Dean Lysyk with a mandate to submit its report by August 1, 1977. In an effort to allay the fears of the northerners, including the native people, and to avert a boycott of the natives who viewed such a short inquiry as a whitewash, the then minister of Indian affairs and northern development assured Yukoners and the Canadian people that a second stage inquiry would be held.

speechtext:
Indeed, the above report goes on to declare:
The inquiry is to submit its report, including the preliminary impact statement, by August 1 in order that its findings may be taken into account by the government in decisions it expects to take concerning northern pipelines in the early autumn.
The minister said that if the Alaska Highway application should receive approval, the government would establish a further inquiry to assist it in developing terms and conditions for the construction and operation of the line. As I indicated earlier, Mr. Speaker, let us make no mistake; Dean Lysyk, when he was travelling through the community, gave the message to every Yukoner, Indian and white alike that in the event that an Alcan pipeline was approved, there would be a second stage inquiry.
It is perfectly clear that this government made a commitment to have a second stage inquiry if the Alaskan Highway application was approved, and yet both the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Faulkner) and the President of Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen) have said no to a second stage public inquiry.
Is it any wonder that the Council of Yukon Indians during their visit to Ottawa stated:
Throughout the inquiry, our people in the communities stated their strong objections to the pipeline proposal. And in every community our people listened as Dean Lysyk repeated the promise of a second stage inquiry. We believed the government and their agent but now we are advised by the Minister of Indian Affairs, Hugh Faulkner, that there will be no second stage inquiry. We have been denied participation in all pipeline discussion. Our hopes for establishing a relationship of trust and co-operation are gone. The wound is deep and the hurt deeper.
On Saturday, February 4, the Toronto Globe and Mail reported the President of Privy Council as stating a second stage inquiry into the impact of the pipeline on the north would not take place. Instead, as reported in the paper, an

advisory committee would be established to obtain public input.
The minister knows such an advisory committee is similar to the "citizens' advisory panel" recommended in the report from the committee on interior and insular affairs of October 25, 1977, entitled "Approving the presidential decision of an Alaska natural gas transportation system and for other purposes." The minister knows that, irrespective of the merits of an advisory committee, it will not replace the second stage inquiry promised by this government that is so crucial to the communities in the Yukon.
Again, Sir, during the fall of 1977, following the decision to build the Alcan pipeline, the Union of B.C. Chiefs, under the able direction of George Manuel, the past president of the National Indian Brotherhood, requested that the second stage inquiry as promised by the government be carried out. With the signing of the agreement between the U.S.A. and Canada, it was now apparent there would be a significant impact on the Indian communities, particularly in the north and east of B.C. in such places as Fort St. John and Fort Nelson.
In anticipation of the disruptive changes which would occur in these Indian communities the Union of B.C. Chiefs made a very sensible and responsible request for a second stage inquiry, which was initially, and I must re-emphasize this, promised by this government. The minister and the government again said no to the B.C. request. The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, the Deputy Prime Minister and the government know that with this change in policy the government has broken its promise. Indians and native people have been betrayed. The government has lost the confidence of native people and, what is more important, the government has imperilled the prospects of a fair and just settlement.
I want to serve notice that at the appropriate time during debate or study of this bill I intend to pursued the important matter of a second stage inquiry, and I hope that during this debate or committee hearings we will be able to convince the government that it should honour its previous commitment to all those in the Yukon and in the northeast part of British Columbia.
When the United States and Canada signed the agreement in principle applicable to a northern natural gas pipeline in September of 1977, agreeing to a timetable for beginning construction of the pipeline in the Yukon by January 1, 1981, they ignored a very significant recommendation of Dean Lysyk. In his chapter on Yukon Indian land claims the third recommendation appearing at page 121 declares, and I quote: For the reasons stated in part E of this chapter, some additional time is desirable to avoid prejudice to a just settlement. Construction of the pipeline should not commence before August 1, 1981.
Dean Lysyk was not recommending a moratorium. He was not recommending some unrealistic time delay; his was a responsible position. He was recommending a responsible time in keeping with the complexities and sensitivity of the issue in the Yukon Territory. Yet this government chose to ignore this
February 15, 1978

important recommendation. As I indicated, that is reminiscent of the days when I asked the former minister of Indian affairs and northern development for a one month extension to complete negotiations on the James Bay settlement.
The legacy of broken promises and delaying tactics of this government unfortunately has transformed negotiation into confrontation. Witness the application for leave to appeal the recommendations of the National Energy Board submitted by the Yukon Conservation Society and the Council of Yukon Indians. If I understand the legislation before us correctly, it blocks entirely a move by any group, including native groups, to have hearings before courts in the future.
The government's game plan is obvious. With the passage of this legislation the momentum of the project will impede efforts to conclude a fair and just settlement. The rights of individuals can be conveniently shunted aside in the name of progress. Dean Lysyk stated in the Alaska Highway pipeline inquiry:
With respect to the Yukon Indian land claim, the proposed pipeline represents both an opportunity and a risk.
The government has failed to understand the significance and importance of that statement. If the past has taught us anything, it is simply that pre-conceived views and unilateral action bear little relation to the real problems of the Indian and native people in Canada. Through broken promises and deliberate attempts to delay the negotiations which commenced in 1973, this government has impeded the prospect of allowing Indian and native people to choose a future path which they, their children and their children's children wish to follow.
The native people are not asking us to determine what the Indian was, what the Indian is today or what he may become in the future. They are simply asking us to accept him as he is and to provide him the choice to develop without interference. I regret to say that that has not occurred under the administration of this government.
