subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF AGENCY TO SUPERVISE PIPELINE CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with regard to the construction of a natural gas pipeline I would like to paraphrase a statement made by the hon. Mr. Justice Berger, who said, and I quote: "The risk is in Canada; the urgency in the United States." I prefer to think that the urgency is in the United States and the opportunity is in the Yukon.
Traditionally pipelines have been powered by the resource being transported through the lines. For example, much of the Alyeska pipeline is powered by the oil running through it. In the case of the proposed natural gas pipeline the intention is to bleed gas from the line in order to operate the driving motors, the compressors. The amount of gas required to drive these motors would be approximately 8 per cent of the gas in the line, or enough gas to heat 750,000 homes annually. At a time when there exists a critical national shortage of natural gas, 8 per cent of the gas in the line used simply to operate the
Northern Pipeline
motors is a tremendous waste which would be better used in the marketplace.
An Anchorage engineering firm, Retherford and Associates, has come up with a more economic means of driving the motors, that being to electrify the pipeline. Electrification of the pipeline in the southern Yukon was previously mentioned by the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen) in his speech opening the debate on this bill on Monday. Electrical energy, either by means of coal, oil, geothermal heat or hydro-electricity, could be used to power the natural gas to its various destinations. Each basic resource was examined to determine the most viable and economic method for electricity production to be used instead of the fuel gas in the gas transport system. The high price of oil, the rising price of coal and the lack of research and development in the area of geothermal heat made it clear that hydroelectricity would be the most feasible and competitive fuel to power the pipeline in the Yukon.
What are the reasons? First, hydroelectric energy can be developed in sufficient quantity at competitive cost. Second, hydroelectric energy is a renewable resource, the fuel of which is descending water, which does not escalate in price and which is not depletable.
Third, the use of hydroelectric energy reduces the pressure on other energy sources and extends the life of non-renewable fuels, the future value of which may lie in other uses more important than energy, such as food.
Fourth, the hydroelectric process is non-polluting.
Fifth, hydroelectric projects have long lives, and their major structures are relatively maintenance free.
Sixth, hydroelectric energy can easily be used instead of fossil fuels such as gas, oil and coal, which can be used in other market areas.
The Yukon has hydroelectric potential, and therefore it is essential that we take this opportunity to capitalize on such an energy swap. In short, the use of hydroelectric power to drive the natural gas pipeline would ensure that an additional 8 per cent of the gas resource would reach the marketplace. Once there, the value of this gas would more than pay the cost of the use of electrical energy.
Moreover, the construction of a dam on the Yukon River to generate this hydroelectricity would give strong assistance to the infrastructure of the Yukon economy. The abundance of hydroelectricity generated would not only drive the motors of the pipeline but also serve the community.
The market for the electricity assured by the electrification of the pipeline would justify the construction of a dam that would generate twice as much electricity as is needed for the pipeline. The remaining 50 per cent electrical capacity would be an extremely valuable aid in the development and advancement of the already existing lines as well as attracting secondary industry, which would not have otherwise come to the area. It would diversify the economic base of the Yukon and

February 15, 1978
Northern Pipeline
would be assured of being readily accepted by the Yukon. For both the dam and the pipeline I feel Canada has the capacity to undergo such an enormous project at a competitive price. We have the Canadian know-how, the competent engineers and technicians; we have the Canadian manpower, a sufficient and able labour force, and we also have Canadian materials sufficient to meet the needs of the proposed pipeline.
I urge the people making the decision on the means of driving the natural gas from Prudhoe Bay to southern markets to investigate very carefully the suggestion of using hydroelectricity as the source of energy. The people of the Yukon await the decision. We have the Canadian talent. We must maximize the potential economic, industrial, energy and social benefits for the Canadian people, while at the same time minimizing adverse social and environmental impacts. This is an excellent opportunity to help in the development of the Yukon and also of Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker. I am terribly excited about the performance of my friend from across the aisle. He has been painting this Utopian dream for the Yukon that we have always known about, and that this government has procrastinated with for the last 100 years. If they had just listened to the Yukon Territorial Council and to the hon. member from the Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) who has spoken about these things for the last 20 years, we would probably have achieved some of these projects long before now.
It is my intention to confine much of my remarks today to purely parochial interests, and I feel justified in doing that, because my constituency, Mr. Speaker, encompasses about one-third of the geography of British Columbia in which 540 miles of this pipeline will be placed. The section which I am concerned with is described in the bill as entering British Columbia near Watson Lake, on the B.C.-Yukon border. It will follow the general route down the Alaska Highway, touching all the small communities along the route, such as Lower Post, Fireside, Summit Lake, Trutch, Fort Nelson and Fort St. John. It will traverse and touch the Stone Mountain and Muncho Lake provincial parks, areas, Mr. Speaker, that have traditionally been the domain of native hunters and trappers, all of whom will be affected by this pipeline, as well as a number of very sensitive game sanctuaries and breeding grounds. Closer to the Peace River country, Mr. Speaker, the pipeline will go through some of British Columbia's most productive farmland before it enters the province of Alberta near Dawson Creek.
Very few of my hon. friends in the House, Mr. Speaker, have heard before all of these exotic places, but that comes as no surprise to me. Unfortunately, there is not enough time for me today to make more than brief reference to this great area of our country.
My hon. friends here will recall my repeated efforts to convince the government to extend the terms of both the Lysyk and the Berger inquiries to study the impact the pipeline will have on the area that I have described; but, as you know, Mr. Speaker, the government chose, as it does in so many things, to

hold the provincial governments in this particular matter responsible for whatever planning or preparation will be necessary to minimize the obvious negative side effects, and, on the other hand, to maximize the positive benefits that could accrue to the area touched by the pipeline. In so doing, the federal government abrogated its clear responsibility in a number of very important areas of their own jurisdiction, and I want to touch on these, Mr. Speaker.
Firstly, the Alaska Highway, or that portion of the highway, namely 600 miles, which travels through British Columbia. As you know, Mr. Speaker, that highway is entirely under federal jurisdiction. It is owned and maintained by the Department of Public Works and will, of course, be the major staging and access route for the pipeline contractors. To a great extent, Mr. Speaker, the highway is used by travellers from the United States since it offers the only road link-between Alaska and the other states south of the 49th parallel.
Many thousands of visitors from all across our country and, indeed, from every corner of the globe travel the highway every year. They come to take part in a unique experience, to see part of our country and its history which most Canadians have already forgotten. They find fulfilment in the rugged wilderness and go to hunt and fish and enjoy the many wilderness scenes and wildlife species, such as the mountain goats, mountain sheep and grizzly bears which still abound in the area. As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, the tourist sector of British Columbia's economy of which the Alaska Highway is a most vital component, is probably the most important industry in that province next to wood fibre and maybe mining.
All of British Columbia's oil and gas deposits are serviced from the Alaska Highway, which provides access for a significant portion of the forest and mining industry in the province as well. The number of people who service and cater to all these industrial and recreational activities is greater than the total population of the Yukon. Every single person will be affected by the pipeline. As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, there are twice the number of people living in the areas of northeastern British Columbia-which I have described-who will be directly affected by the pipeline than there are in the area of our country which was studied by the Berger and Lysyk inquiries at a cost of tens of millions of dollars. Some of these people, Mr. Speaker, are of native ancestry, and again the numbers are at least equal to those to whom all the attention of the inquiry was directed.
Now surely, Mr. Speaker, the government cannot deny its direct responsibility, at least in the area of native concerns. If there is such a thing as special rights and aboriginal title for native people, the government of British Columbia has never heard of it. If there is a special deal for native people, Mr. Speaker, it is a deal they must address to the federal government. As far as British Columbia is concerned, even the reservations that have been set aside for the native people in that area can be expropriated for railway rights-of-way, roads and power installations. That has been done. As my hon. friends know, there were no treaties with the Indians in most of British Columbia. As far as the Peace River country is
February 15, 1978

concerned, however, we do have treaty No. 8, and it will form the basis on which the natives of northern British Columbia are beginning to build their case-and I hate to say it- against the pipeline.
I fully understand all of the difficulties the companies will experience if they do not receive approval by March of this year to finalize their plans and to start working on the logistics of building the line. 1 understand as well the problems the government faces if the pipeline agreement is not ratified by parliament before an election is called. But, Mr. Speaker, I am at this time in no position to sympathize with these problems. You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that I was one of the first to greet the National Energy Board's decision to opt for the Alcan route instead of the Mackenzie Valley route with a great deal of excitement and enthusiasm. You will also recall, however, Mr. Speaker, that I urged the government repeatedly to begin their discussions with the government - of British Columbia and assess the problems, in socioeconomic terms, in the areas affected by the pipeline.
On April 22 last year I raised a question in this House to find out whether the terms of reference of the Lysyk inquiry in the Yukon could be extended. 1 asked the government this question on July 18, October 6, October 26 and December 19. Twice within the last couple of weeks I have used my time in the House during question period to remind the government of their direct responsibilities in this regard. I have asked the government to table the agreements which they have reached with the province of British Columbia so that we can intelligently and adequately discuss them here in the House. I have asked the Government through local, regional and municipal authorities as well as citizens groups to safeguard against any unnecessary and negative side effect.
Unfortunately these legitimate requests have so far been ignored. There has been no dialogue as far as I am concerned with the agencies I have mentioned. Whatever discussions have been held with the province have been held behind closed doors. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, the agreement with the United States requires a statement of acquiescence from the provinces affected by the pipeline. The B.C. government gave its approval without any consultation with local governments and without any formal study or inquiry into the possible impact of the project.
I am put in the position today of making a judgment on behalf of my constituents without even knowing what demands or conditions the government of British Columbia has placed on the building of a pipeline or approval of it. As part of the agreement between Canada and the United States these statements of concurrence must be issued. Let me state what the bill says in respect to the British Columbia situation:
Specific details of this undertaking will be the subject of a federal-provincial agreement to be negotiated at as early a date as possible. Such agreement should guarantee that British Columbia's position expressed in its telex of August 31 is protected.
You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that I asked the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen) whether he would be prepared to
Northern Pipeline
table the communique. On two occasions, the hon. gentleman preferred not to make this document public. Whenever the government is reluctant to pass on information, I am suspicious that they have something to hide. From the point of view of myself and my constituents, it would appear that the bill will have to wait until the two governments consider it timely to tell those people who have to live with this extravagant scheme, both during and after construction, how their environment, their lives and their future will be affected.
I do not trust either this government or the government of British Columbia with such an important and far-reaching decision. In northern British Columbia we have been disappointed before. For instance, we were told that the total work force of 6,000 men, which at one time was working on the Peace River dam project, would find work in industry attracted to the area by the government. They would be able to take advantage of the special on-site power rates. As well local municipalities and communities would have access to the preferred power rates, easing the burden of building the required infrastructure.
Over 600 square miles of land was flooded, with monstrous environmental and ecological consequences. None of the promises was kept. Power rates in the Peace River country are still higher today than they are in Vancouver which is 700 miles away. The federal government failed to exercise any of its jurisdiction when whole settlements of Indians were forced off their land without compensation. These included registered reservations. The massive body of water has affected the climate and atmospheric conditions in the area to the point where it has seriously threatened the viability of certain industries. The growing of certain cereal crops in the Peace River area is a marginal endeavour today. I am always sceptical when this government makes any deals, the terms of which cannot be made public.
My concern in respect to this project is somewhat different from those expressed by most of our colleagues. Like the territorial council of the Yukon, I worry about the impact on the local labour market as much as I do about assuring Canadian content, which is most important. I want similar assurances to those granted to the Yukon in respect to preferential treatment of local workers, businessmen and entrepreneurs.
On the other hand, 1 know what it means to local employers. Local industry will not be able to match the lucrative labour contracts. Machine operators and workers will enjoy higher wages as a result of these contracts during the pipeline construction. Labourers of all categories will seek work connected with the pipeline construction and will quit their present jobs. Local businesses will be forced to raise their wages in order to equal wages being paid by the pipeline companies. Alternatively, they will close down for lack of workers.
I took a trip last summer through Alaska and the Yukon to study the impact of the pipeline on the communities along the Alyeska route. I was told that in Fairbanks 80 per cent of the municipal police force left their jobs to work on the pipeline construction just at the time when the drug peddlers, gamblers

February 15, 1978
Northern Pipeline
and prostitutes arrived. An acute shortage of labour will occur in the local area whenever such a large project commences. Local residents will be denied their most essential services.
Experience along the Alyeska route as well shows that the contractors like to use local supplies and service facilities as much as possible. However, these facilities are always inadequate, and there is a lack of time to gear up for the influx of new business. When the projects are completed it will take months if not years to get everything back to normal, as was the case in Alaska. During construction of the pipeline it will be worth one's life to travel the Alaska highway. The term "highway" is too generous a description of the road which was built in 1942 by the United States army as a defence project. For the most part it is a dirt road. The federal government has plans to upgrade and pave the road; however, this has never been a priority. My hon. friends and colleagues will recall the many interventions I have made in the House in support of an accelerated upgrading program for the highway. The paving from Fort St. John to Fort Nelson was to be completed this year, but it will now take an all-out effort to come close to completing that section to coincide with the completion of the construction of the pipeline.
The adjustments that will have to be made by the smaller communities is a concern of mine. They must accommodate the influx of population required to maintain and operate the line once it is in place. We know of the commitment made by the provinces not to levy additional taxes or fees, which was commensurate with the commitment made in the bilateral agreement. There is no mention made of who is to pay for the additional services required by towns, cities and villages along the way, including schools, hospitals and recreational facilities which the newcomers have a right to demand. Will their cost be borne by the local taxpayers? We do not know that. We expect cost is a component of the behind the door agreement reached with the province of British Columbia.
Again, Mr. Speaker, our previous experience provides us with little comfort. Governments have always been more preoccupied with calculating royalties and taxes than with assuring those people who manned the frontier and maintained the facilities in remote areas of equitable living conditions.
I would be remiss if I did not recognize the exemplary corporate citizenship demonstrated by one of the partners in the Foothills consortium, namely Westcoast Transmission. This company, as you know, Mr. Speaker, is taking part in the pipeline construction. It has built and it maintains hundreds of miles of pipeline in British Columbia. Where the government neglected their responsibility, the company took over, providing housing and recreational facilities, co-operating with local municipal councils and community groups, encouraging their employees to integrate, to take part in the social affairs of their new towns.
In some cases brand new small communities had to be built, but wherever possible the employees live in existing towns, adding to their vibrancy and viability. This company has a

unique and enviable relationship with their employees as well. Their industrial relations process could serve as a model to most other industries, and even to the government in its dealings with the public service.
I encourage hon. members to study what Westcoast Transmission is doing for its employees. It was the the officials of Westcoast Transmission who made the first and only contact with the municipal and regional officials, discussing the new project and its implications. However, this dialogue is limited in the sense that the company as well can only speculate on the terms of reference the government will eventually dictate and the guidelines that must be followed. At this point they have not been told what size of pipe they must use for the project. They have been told that they must bear the costs of the monitoring agency, but there is no indication of the size or dimension of the bureaucracy. The company knows that the British Columbia government will attache certain conditions on the permits they must issue, but no one knows what these conditions might be.
Frankly, Mr. Speaker, I wonder why the private sector still gets involved at all in such risky schemes. The risks are not any abnormal or changing market conditions or unknown factors in respect to the technological challenges connected to the resource harvest in the new frontier and hostile environments, but rather the risks of dealing with governments which make their own rules as they go along, usually after irreversible commitments have been made by the resource sector, governments that regulate and change at whim every aspect of market conditions.
Government estimates on which their policy decisions in the public interest are based are consistently and hopelessly wrong. A year ago, for instance, we were told that we might be experiencing serious shortages in natural gas in the early eighties. That was only five years after the government declared that our domestic requirements are secure for the next 100 years. The latest estimates announced by the policymakers of the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources show that we will have no trouble meeting both our domestic and export commitments with reserves already identified until at least 1990.
I wonder what impact those latest inventory figures will have on pipeline decisions. How firm, for instance, is the agreement with the U.S. which is annexed to the bill under schedule I? With respect to the schedules of construction, we do not know and probably will not know until long after this bill is passed in this House just what is involved.
The passing of Bill C-25 will not answer any of the questions that need to be answered before the companies can proceed with their final plans. The passing of this bill will not facilitate the assembly of the capital required to build the line.
What it will do, however, is give the government the opportunity to make all other remaining and critical decisions without the scrutiny of parliament. It will give the government the option to make final decisions respecting Canadian content of labour and supplies, and critical decisions respecting timing and the staging of the various sections in a manner that
February 15, 1978

accommodates their political objectives and the timing of this year's election.
Most of my constituents welcome the pipeline. We in northeastern British Columbia have learned to appreciate the major influence this industry has had in the economy of the north and the quality of life. The industry has helped to stabilize small and fragile communities, adding an important tax base to the marginal source of finances available. The pipelines and processing facilities have added an important dimension to the job markets. They have opened up the country, helping to provide access to other resources in the area.
While there is always an upheaval during construction, it can well be said that there are no harmful side effects in terms of the environment. Even the wildlife has adjusted well to the rights-of-way which provide additional food and trails for the animals to get around. But in spite of all that, we do not want the pipeline at just any price. We must have some assurances, similar to those built into the bill for the Yukon, that the existing communities will receive adequate help to cope with the pressures and social tensions that will accrue during the construction period.
We want local residents to have preferential treatment when applying for the construction jobs. Local business entrepreneurs must be given the opportunity to supply all those services they are capable of supplying. We must insist that the contractors and the companies operating the system once it is in place will make every effort to train young people, particularly young native people, in the skills they require; and, most important, we want the infrastructure around the project built to accommodate the needs and the legitimate aspirations of the people already in the area.
With regard to the labour component, one of the most necessary matters that has not been mentioned is the fact that there needs to be an agreement with the unions for access to their membership on the part of local residents so that they can be placed on these important jobs.
Ironically, most of these demands can be met without any additional costs to the project. As a matter of fact, with the least degree of foresight and planning the objectives of all concerned could be made to complement each other. For instance, the operation of the system will require a very sophisticated communications system employing the latest technology. This system, if properly planned, could, without much additional cost, carry radio, television and telephone channels and signals which could service the residential settlements along the route. These services are presently not available for the most part of the highway area. With a small number of strategically located breakout systems, the whole area could be serviced with these essential amenities which other Canadians have taken for granted for two generations. Similarly, access routes and transportation infrastructure could be planned commensurate with other interests.
Without the benefit of an impact study which would directly relate to the pipeline, I must rely on my experience in municipal and regional governments and on the studies that have
Northern Pipeline
been made by the various authorities in the areas affected, such as chambers of commerce and councils.
I must assume, that we can rely on the province to provide and advance the funds required for the initial adjustment that local settlements must make. The sum of $200 million, which is the figure used in the Yukon, is not unrealistic for northeastern British Columbia.
We must insist on a firm commitment to build in the cost of laterals to service the settlements north of Fort Nelson and to adjust the rates charged in Fort Nelson commensurate with Alberta border prices.
There must be an immediate assessment of any land claims that may arise and an effort to begin negotiations. In addition to that, however, there must be a clear commitment by the federal government to accelerate the reconstruction program on the Alaska Highway to the point where it is paved to mile 315, which is the junction with the Liard Highway. As well, we want to know the role the B.C. railway will play in the staging and transport scheme. There is a great deal of uncertainty about the future of that part of the railway which spans the stretch from Fort St. John to Fort Nelson. In view of the importance of this rail link to industries in Fort Nelson, we want the rail bed upgraded not only to accommodate the pipeline contractors but also to assure continued service to the vital resource areas of the north. I can only hope that all these points are incorporated in the provincial shopping list when it is finally made public.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, it is the intention of my party to expedite the bill in every way possible having regard to the many opportunities which can accrue to Canadian business and labour as a result of the project. I would point out, however, that the government has had this legislation ready for four months. It could have been debated at the time the United States Congress dealt with the matter. We are now called upon to proceed with almost indecent haste in our consideration of the bill while assuring adequate safeguards for Canadian interests. My hon. friends have drawn attention to many areas in which the bill is imperfect. As one editorial said this morning, there are so many holes in this bill it could accommodate a pipeline.
I serve notice on the government that ministers will have to be much more co-operative during the committee proceedings, much more free with information, if they wish to ensure our support. To those members on the government side who would like to blame us for holding up this bill, I say that the people who will be holding up the bill will be the natives in the Yukon and in northeastern British Columbia who will be sitting in courtrooms and in front of bulldozers because they realize that, once again, their last chance of seeing the promises made to them by the government fulfilled has gone by. We on this side intend to insist on significant changes being made in this bill, so it is really up to the government to decide when the legislation will leave the House and when the contractors will be able to get on with their work.

Northern Pipeline

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the note on which my hon. friend from Prince George-Peace River (Mr. Oberle) concluded is the note on which I feel I should begin. This is beyond any question one of the most questionable operations the government has tried to pull off. I refer to the manner in which the introduction of the bill has been delayed.

speechtext: Thank you!

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF AGENCY TO SUPERVISE PIPELINE CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
The agreement with the United States was signed on September 20 in this city. The bill was introduced on February 6. There was plenty of lead time, even as the agreement was being concluded, to have prepared a measure for implementation in legislative form to be placed before the House.
I have noticed that this is not the first time the government has exercised a delaying device of this sort for the single purpose of trying to secure a political advantage by forcing the opposition to make hasty decisions. We have had six days only in which to examine this legislation. It is an important bill. Aside from the other bill which we considered earlier this session in relation to the budget and granting the government authority to borrow $10 billion, it is the only bill to come before us which deals with a sum of this magnitude. Here is another bill which involves $10 billion. Not all of that sum, it is true, is to be raised by Canadians but we are dealing with issues of a magnitude which cannot be overlooked.
This party, the party to our left and the party down at the end of the chamber have had six days in which to study the implications of this bill, yet we are being pushed to allow the measure through. We have given an undertaking that we shall not delay the measure in the House. But I still believe every member on this side should make it clear that bills of this importance should not become the political playthings of the government. This is not the way to govern a country as delicate as Canada. I find it shameful that there should be members sitting in this chamber today who can accept that sort of thing. It is deplorable. It is a form of blackmail.
[ Translation]
Aside from that, I have other remarks to make and having commented on that matter, I would like to add that we all want to be sure that Canadian manpower and industries will be involved to the highest degree possible in the construction and maintenance of the proposed pipeline. It is a huge project, Mr. Speaker, since it is expected to cost $10 billion and require a construction period of two to three years as well as the use of pipes in Canadian territory over hundreds of miles-1 do not remember exactly how many-a number of miles in Yukon, my colleague just said 600 miles in British Columbia and the rest in the province of Alberta. It is therefore a huge project and we on this side insist, as do government members, I hope,
[Mr. Oberle.)
that Canadian manpower and industry take maximum part in that project.
We want the construction company to be obliged to hire manpower in every part of Canada and also order the needed materials from each of our regions. Let us take advantage of the expertise and steel technology developed not only in Ontario, in Saskatchewan and the west, but also in the province of Quebec and in Nova Scotia. All Canada, Mr. Speaker, must benefit from that huge project. To be sure that it will be so-

-that the future may unfold as it should, Mr. Speaker- [Translation]
-we, of the Progressive Conservative party, will propose to the committee that a monitoring agency accountable to parliament, whether it is a select committee or one of the standing committees of the House, be set up to make sure that the company is complying with the provisions of the bill.
Before turning to another aspect for which I am responsible, namely the environmental problems relating to this matter- and that is my principal task-let me speak of another concern I am most anxious to get on the record. I refer to the opportunities Canadians ought to have of acquiring equity shares in the company responsible for the construction and operation of a pipeline project of this sort and size.
This situation did not arise in the first instance as a result of an earlier pipeline construction, but it did finally occur as a result of a good deal of effort on the part of this party. Our party down through the years has been in the vanguard of those who have sought ways to assure that Canadians have an even, and even a better than even, chance to participate in the fruits of this country's good fortune, not through agencies such as FIRA, but through an ability to participate in projects which have Canada as their base.
A method of assurance would be to require that there be an offer of equity shares in the Foothills pipeline project. Probably Foothills will set up another company in which Canadians should have the opportunity of sharing. This will be a gilt-edge investment if we believe in the future of this country. Why should Canadians not be given the first opportunity to share in and enjoy the benefits that will be accruing to our country once gas begins to flow through the pipeline we are now discussing? The investment will be even more gilt-edged once Canadian gas is flowing through the pipeline, as is hopefully foreseen down the road and 1 will return to that later. 1 should like to see assurances built into this legislation which would give that right to Canadians to participate financially in this great venture and draw profit from it. This is a matter we might well examine more closely once we get into committee.
In referring to the matter of Canadian input of work and material, I would mention the need for a parliamentary monitoring agency which would be required on a quarterly basis to
February 15, 1978

keep under scrutiny the manner in which the many varied terms and conditions imposed on the construction companies and others under the bill are being carried out. This project is too vast to think that parliament in a matter of a week, two weeks or three could discuss it, pass it and forget about it, going on to something else. We have to be able to come back to this project to make sure that what we have stipulated is being carried out. We cannot just say: "There you are, we have passed the bill, now you get on with it". We have to be able to assure ourselves and Canadians that those who are authorized under the bill to do the job will do it in a manner that is wholly and in every respect consistent with the requirements of this bill. Nothing can be left to chance or to a monitoring agency that cannot be called to account.
The monitoring agency that is envisaged in the bill is an agency which, under these provisions, cannot be called to account. We as members of parliament can and ought to be called to account. That is why we are here. We cannot authorize a project of this size on the basis of allowing things to go ahead without being sure there is some manner in which we can call the company or companies to account for their actions in relation to the legislation. We as parliamentarians should be ready to provide answers when we are called upon to do so. The only way we can do that is by making sure there is an agency in place that will allow us to determine whether, in each particular area of construction, progress is being made along that foreseen critical path, and in accordance with the provisions so loudly being touted regarding the competitive capability of Canadians to provide the materials and workmen.
There must be a more than equal opportunity for Canadians to participate in that construction in Canada. These are matters for which we in this House will be held accountable, and we must be sure we have all the answers. We do not want to be like this government which stands up during the question period and sidesteps questions. We cannot sidestep questions on a matter of this importance. We have to know what is taking place and that it is taking place in a proper way and at the rate it should be taking place in order to produce the greatest economic return possible to this country. A monitoring agency composed of members of this parliament is essential to this whole deal.
We have been talking in general terms about some of the problems that will be faced during construction. Let us consider the things that have yet to be done before the project can get underway. What provisions are there in the bill which give an ironclad assurance that these things will be carried out before the project begins? What about all those things that have to be done before the project materializes?
Let me quote briefly from one of the reports that fortunately was prepared by the environmental assessment panel which in itself was rushed into preparing its assessment of the impact of the project in federally owned territory. I have with me the Hill report. It is an interim report of the environmental assessment panel sent to the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment (Mr. LeBlanc) in July 1977. It was commissioned, if I remember correctly, in February. The panel had a
Northern Pipeline
matter of three or four months to examine and outline those areas where there could possibly be an impact, and then submit recommendations to the minister on what might be done. At page 3 of this particular report the authors state:
The short lead time available made a normal environmental assessment of the project impossible at this time.
That suggests to me that if it was impossible at that time there must be a further study in order that a full environmental assessment can be made. Instead, the panel was instructed to review the existing data, seek public and professional information and submit an interim report by August 1. It did that, but this was purely an interim report.
Yesterday, if I am not mistaken, I heard the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Faulkner) make reference to guidelines following the publication of this report. As yet I have not seen those guidelines. A lot of documentation has crossed my desk relating to the pipeline, among other things, and perhaps I overlooked the guidelines. This environmental panel studied the situation as carefully as it could in the time available. If it produced a set of guidelines which would be of assistance to the construction company, then they should be available to all hon. members who are considering this important piece of legislation.
How can the government expect the House to pass the bill as quickly as possible when some of the documents are not available? There are some things which all hon. members must know before considering this piece of legislation. The hon. member for Prince George-Peace River referred to the position of British Columbia which was sent in a telex to the federal government on August 31. As yet, we do not know what the position of that province is.
It will be necessary to conclude three agreements between the federal government and the provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan and British Columbia. Surely the conditions under which those three provinces agree to the construction of the pipeline are relevant to this debate. Yet we do not have that information. In fact, there are many lacunae in the documentation which is at our disposal. Even so, we are expected to approve this legislation on a crash basis.
I should like to refer to the environmental concerns which the Hill panel laid before us. As I have suggested, the panel was under the gun just as hon. members are. It is unfair to parliament and it is cynical of the government to push the passage of this bill. The importance of the concerns expressed in the Hill report should not be underrated. Environmental concerns are of prime importance. It is only within the past 20 or 30 years that the true significance of the effect that developmental projects can have on the environment has come to light. It is not easy to define the dilemma faced by our modern society when developmental projects begin to manifest an impact on the environment of an affected area. The trouble is that some of the environmental effects need not be immediate. It may take years for the effects to show. The environment must be safeguarded and the developmental change must be allowed.

Northern Pipeline
I happened to notice a cartoon by Norris of the Vancouver Sun which appeared in an Ottawa newspaper. The cartoon depicted a cave situation. There was a bush fire at the mouth of the cave. There were a couple of hairy boys entering the cave wearing goatskins and carrying clubs over their shoulders. At the same time, an equally hairy individual was leaving the cave. Obviously he was an egghead, a man who had been thinking. He had produced an object which the other cavemen were looking at. The caption under the cartoon was: "You can call it a wheel if you like, but to me it is development". Following that, the other cavemen went through the process of breaking it up. Surely that is not the attitude toward development we have to adopt.
I wonder if the definitions of the hon. Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) should be applied to environmental problems. After the federal-provincial meeting of industry ministers on January 30, the minister said that the over-zealous protection of the environment costs jobs. Is that the definition used by the government? Also he said that we, the Canadian people, have to be fully aware of that, and that minimum standards of environmental protection across the country are not necessary, that over-zealous maintenance of minimum standards hurts the regions. Then the minister went on to explain that in areas where there is no industry, standards designed for urban Canada would be inappropriate. Perhaps a pragmatic approach has to be taken. However, there are minimum standards which must be followed. It is a very delicate balance.
I should like to refer to some of the problem areas indicated in the Hill report. The report indicated that there would be damage in various areas that could be mitigated. Also in the final analysis it was indicated that more study was necessary and more data had to be collected before a final decision or recommendation could be reached. Because of the size of the project, its impact in environmental terms will be of the same relative magnitude, according to the report.
The panel referred to the potential environmental effects associated with a buried gas pipeline passing through areas subject to permafrost. They were not examining, they were just spotting. Then they spotted another one, the relative importance of environmental problems resulting from the operation of the chilled line, on one hand, compared with the heated gas mode over the remainder of the route, on the other. With the chilled line, frost accumulation could result in heaving of the pipe, while a warm line could result in the degradation of the surrounding permafrost. These are the sorts of problems that the Hill report saw emerging once the construction was underway.
There is also the possibility of a pipeline rupture due to seismic activities. One of the lines went through a seismic area, and, incidentally, that was the Alcan route. The other line does not go through a seismic area, but there were dangers which they foresaw and which they spotted.

When they were examining the company and its knowledge of the various construction problems, they were advised during the hearings that the proponent had limited knowledge of the occurrence, distribution and nature of permafrost along the proposed route. If I remember correctly, the construction is not likely to begin until about January 1, 1981. There is a two-year lead time.
Mr. Speaker, I wonder if the conversation which is going on across the way might not take place behind the curtains?

speechtext: Will the hon. members please carry on their conversation behind the curtains.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF AGENCY TO SUPERVISE PIPELINE CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
This is another area where the Hill assessment group spotted problems that were going to occur. Another one is river crossings. Should the pipeline be buried under the river or should it be carried by an elevated mode across the river? Because by burying it, there could be damage to it and interference with fish spawning, migration and overwintering and possible deleterious effects of siltation on fish and fish habitat, and the possibility of gas leaks under ice cover. All these are matters which must be investigated.
This is one reason among many that I have maintained from the beginning that a monitoring agency should be set up composed of members of parliament, so that we can be assured that the construction company is examining these matters and making sure that the environmental damage is reduced to the minimum, in a manner which will permit construction to go through. If they have to examine rivers for fish spawning, etc., are they doing it now? We do not know that. I think we should know whether or not they have started this.
There is a provision in the bill at page 50, schedule III, clause 7, which reads as follows:
The company shall, in respect of social and economic matters and environmental, fisheries and agricultural concerns, comply with the undertakings given by Foothills Pipe Lines (Yukon) Ltd., the Alberta Gas Trunk Line (Canada) Limited, Westcoast Transmission Company Limited, and Alberta Natural Gas Company Ltd., and in the submission of the Alberta Gas Trunk Line Company Limited to the board, as amended during the hearing or such orders or directions as may be made or given by the designated officer.
Clause 8 reads:
Prior to the approval of the final detailed design of each section or part of the pipeline, the company shall submit to the designated officer,
(a)	the results of such further studies in respect of social and economic
matters, environmental, fisheries and agricultural concerns as may be ordered
or directed by the designated officer; and
(b)	the recommendations of its environmental consultants for the protection of
fisheries, farm lands and the environment.
These requirements are written into the bill and the provisions are under the general direction of what is known as the designated officer. However, that does not relieve those of us who sit in this parliament of the responsibility to ensure that those requirements are fulfilled. I think in a matter of such importance and size it would be a mistake for us to proceed as though, once the bill has left us and gone to the other place and been given royal assent, it were no longer our concern. It is
February 15, 1978

our concern and it is the concern of the Canadian people. They are going to hold us accountable and we should be in a position to be accountable.
May I call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker?
